sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A relational database stores facts in tables. A row describes one thing; a column describes one property. A DBMS is the software that stores, protects, and queries those facts.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared structure lets many applications agree on names and data types without duplicating the facts.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SELECT chooses columns. FROM names a table. A semicolon ends the statement. PostgreSQL is the DBMS used throughout this course.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
SELECT chooses columns. FROM names a table. A semicolon ends the statement. PostgreSQL is the DBMS used throughout this course.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return every column of customers, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return id, customer_id, ordered_on, status, and total from orders, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered_on, status, total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A primary key identifies one row. A foreign key points to a row in another table. A schema is a namespace containing tables and other objects.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Keys connect facts without copying a customer name into every order. Constraints reject relationships that cannot be valid. Relationship map: customers.id (one) → orders.customer_id (many); orders.id (one) → order_items.order_id (many); products.id (one) → order_items.product_id (many).

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: customers.id is unique. orders.customer_id refers to customers.id and may be NULL for a guest order. order_items has a two-column primary key.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
customers.id is unique. orders.customer_id refers to customers.id and may be NULL for a guest order. order_items has a two-column primary key.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id and name from customers, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return order_id, product_id, and quantity from order_items, ordered by order_id then product_id.
sections.code: SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, product_id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An expression computes a value. SQL is declarative: you describe the answer rather than a loop through the data.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: The database can choose an efficient plan while preserving the meaning of your query.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The logical pipeline starts with FROM and WHERE, then grouping and HAVING, then SELECT, DISTINCT, ordering, and limiting. The physical plan may differ.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
The logical pipeline starts with FROM and WHERE, then grouping and HAVING, then SELECT, DISTINCT, ordering, and limiting. The physical plan may differ.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
sections.code: SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 AS answer;

sections.title: A small example

sections.code: SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 AS answer;

sections.title: A realistic use

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Projection means choosing the columns of the result. An alias gives a result column a clear name.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A focused result is easier to read, uses less transfer, and makes an application contract explicit.

sections.title: How it works

• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows after the output expressions have been evaluated.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports often need unique categories rather than one row for every product.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DISTINCT applies to the entire selected row, not just the first selected column. NULLs are treated as equal for duplicate elimination.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
DISTINCT applies to the entire selected row, not just the first selected column. NULLs are treated as equal for duplicate elimination.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return distinct product category values, ordered alphabetically.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return distinct month numbers as month and status from orders, ordered by month and status.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM ordered_on)::integer AS month, status FROM orders ORDER BY month, status;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: ORDER BY establishes a result order. LIMIT chooses a maximum number of rows; OFFSET skips rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Pagination and top-N reports need a predictable ordering contract.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Sort keys are evaluated left to right. DESC reverses one key. Add a unique tie-breaker to make limited results deterministic.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Sort keys are evaluated left to right. DESC reverses one key. Add a unique tie-breaker to make limited results deterministic.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
• LIMIT restricts the row count after ordering; a deterministic tie-breaker makes that choice reproducible.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: NULL represents a missing or unknown value. It is not zero, an empty string, or a special ordinary value.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Real data often has unknown shipment dates or optional contact details. SQL keeps that uncertainty visible.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. WHERE keeps true only; false and unknown are discarded. IS DISTINCT FROM compares NULLs as values.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. WHERE keeps true only; false and unknown are discarded. IS DISTINCT FROM compares NULLs as values.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: LIKE matches a pattern. Percent matches any string; underscore matches one character. PostgreSQL ILIKE ignores case according to locale.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Text searches often need prefixes, suffixes, and case-insensitive matching.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Surround a fragment with percent signs for contains. Escape wildcard characters when they must match literally.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Surround a fragment with percent signs for contains. Escape wildcard characters when they must match literally.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: A realistic use

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A regular expression describes a richer text pattern than LIKE. PostgreSQL uses POSIX-style regular expressions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Validation and extraction sometimes need character classes, repetition, and boundaries.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The ~ operator matches case-sensitively; ~* ignores case. Anchors ^ and $ mark the beginning and end.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
The ~ operator matches case-sensitively; ~* ignores case. Anchors ^ and $ mark the beginning and end.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: CASE returns a value chosen by conditions. It is an expression and can appear wherever a value is needed.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports translate raw values into useful business labels without changing the source rows.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Searched CASE tests WHEN conditions in order and returns the first matching THEN value. ELSE handles the remaining cases.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Searched CASE tests WHEN conditions in order and returns the first matching THEN value. ELSE handles the remaining cases.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id, CASE WHEN stock = 0 THEN 'empty' WHEN stock < 10 THEN 'low' ELSE 'ready' END AS stock_status FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: FILTER applies a condition to one aggregate. CASE inside an aggregate is another way to express conditional summaries.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A dashboard can compare several segments in one result without running separate queries.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Write aggregate(...) FILTER (WHERE condition). The outer WHERE still filters the input for every aggregate.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Write aggregate(...) FILTER (WHERE condition). The outer WHERE still filters the input for every aggregate.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: GROUP BY forms groups of rows that share grouping values, then calculates aggregates for each group.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Category and department summaries answer business questions at a different level of detail.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Every output expression must be grouped or aggregated, except columns that PostgreSQL can prove functionally dependent on grouped primary keys.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Every output expression must be grouped or aggregated, except columns that PostgreSQL can prove functionally dependent on grouped primary keys.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return category and product_count for each category, ordered by category.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return department, employee_count, and average_salary rounded to two decimals, ordered by department.
sections.code: SELECT department, count(*) AS employee_count, round(avg(salary),2) AS average_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY department;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: HAVING filters completed groups using aggregate conditions. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report can show only categories with enough products or customers with meaningful spending.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Place HAVING after GROUP BY. Aggregate conditions belong here; ordinary row restrictions usually belong in WHERE.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Place HAVING after GROUP BY. Aggregate conditions belong here; ordinary row restrictions usually belong in WHERE.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• HAVING filters whole groups after their aggregates are known.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING count(*) >= 3 ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return category and product_count for categories with at least 3 products, ordered by category.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING count(*) >= 3 ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return customer_id and spend for known customers with paid order totals above 100, ordered by customer_id.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS spend FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id HAVING sum(total) > 100 ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Grouping sets compute several grouping levels in one query. ROLLUP adds hierarchical subtotals; CUBE adds every combination.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report can include details and totals while keeping one source definition.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GROUPING(column) returns 1 when that column is absent from a subtotal grouping set. It distinguishes subtotal NULL from a genuine NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
GROUPING(column) returns 1 when that column is absent from a subtotal grouping set. It distinguishes subtotal NULL from a genuine NULL.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT category, sum(stock) AS units, grouping(category) AS is_total FROM products GROUP BY ROLLUP(category) ORDER BY is_total, category;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A join combines rows from two data sources. INNER JOIN keeps pairs whose ON condition is true.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Related facts can stay in separate normalized tables and still appear together in a report.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Name each source, give it a short alias, and connect its key columns with ON. One input row can match zero, one, or many rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Name each source, give it a short alias, and connect its key columns with ON. One input row can match zero, one, or many rows.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, o.total FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return order id as order_id, customer name as customer, and total for orders with a known customer, ordered by order id.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, o.total FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return product_id, product name as product, warehouse, and value (inventory quantity times product price), ordered by product_id.
sections.code: SELECT i.product_id, p.name AS product, i.warehouse, i.quantity * p.price AS value FROM inventory i JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id ORDER BY i.product_id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: LEFT JOIN keeps every left row. If no right row matches, its right-side output columns are NULL.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A customer without orders still belongs in an account report.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use LEFT JOIN ... ON. A right-side condition in ON limits matches; a right-side condition in WHERE can remove unmatched left rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use LEFT JOIN ... ON. A right-side condition in ON limits matches; a right-side condition in WHERE can remove unmatched left rows.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return customer id as customer_id and order id as order_id, preserving customers with no orders; order by customer_id then order_id NULLS LAST.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return customer id as customer_id and paid_count, including every customer, ordered by customer id. Restrict paid status in the join condition.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, count(o.id) AS paid_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: RIGHT JOIN preserves the right source. FULL JOIN preserves both sources. CROSS JOIN produces every possible pair.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reconciliation needs unmatched rows from both lists; planning sometimes needs every combination.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Outer joins add NULL values for the missing side. CROSS JOIN has no ON predicate. RIGHT JOIN can usually be rewritten by swapping a LEFT JOIN.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Outer joins add NULL values for the missing side. CROSS JOIN has no ON predicate. RIGHT JOIN can usually be rewritten by swapping a LEFT JOIN.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id FROM orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A self join gives the same table two aliases so one row can refer to another row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Employees and managers share the same row structure but play different roles in a report.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Join employee.manager_id to manager.id. Use LEFT JOIN when the top-level employee has no manager.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Join employee.manager_id to manager.id. Use LEFT JOIN when the top-level employee has no manager.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT e.id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return employee id, employee name as employee, and manager name as manager, including the top-level employee; order by employee id.
sections.code: SELECT e.id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id;

sections.title: A realistic use

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: EXISTS checks whether a subquery produces at least one row. NOT EXISTS checks that it produces none.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Existence questions should not multiply the output when many matches exist.

sections.title: How it works

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A derived table is a subquery in FROM. LATERAL lets that subquery refer to preceding FROM sources.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Each customer may need a small related result such as their most recent order.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Alias every derived table for clarity. LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true preserves outer rows with no inner result.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Alias every derived table for clarity. LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true preserves outer rows with no inner result.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
sections.code: SELECT round(avg(order_count),2) AS average_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) counts;

sections.title: A small example

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A common table expression, or CTE, names a query for use within a larger statement.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Named stages make a complicated reporting calculation easier to reason about.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: WITH name AS (...) introduces a CTE before the main query. PostgreSQL can fold some CTEs into the parent query; MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED influence that behavior.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
WITH name AS (...) introduces a CTE before the main query. PostgreSQL can fold some CTEs into the parent query; MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED influence that behavior.

• WITH gives a query stage a name; the final SELECT reads its output.
• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: WITH paid AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') SELECT id, total FROM paid WHERE total > 50 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Use a CTE to return id and total for paid orders over 50, ordered by id.
sections.code: WITH paid AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') SELECT id, total FROM paid WHERE total > 50 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return category and revenue for categories whose paid line revenue exceeds the mean category revenue, ordered by category.
sections.code: WITH category_sales AS (SELECT p.category, sum(i.quantity*i.unit_price) AS revenue FROM products p JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id=p.id JOIN orders o ON o.id=i.order_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category) SELECT category, revenue FROM category_sales WHERE revenue > (SELECT avg(revenue) FROM category_sales) ORDER BY category;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: UNION combines compatible results and removes duplicates. UNION ALL preserves every input row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Data from separate segments can be combined using the same output contract.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each branch needs the same number of columns and compatible data types. The first branch determines result column names.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Each branch needs the same number of columns and compatible data types. The first branch determines result column names.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT city AS place FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL UNION SELECT warehouse FROM inventory ORDER BY place;

sections.title: A small example

sections.code: SELECT city AS place FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL UNION SELECT warehouse FROM inventory ORDER BY place;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return source and amount for paid order totals (source order) and all booking charges (source booking), preserving all rows; order by source then amount.
sections.code: SELECT 'order' AS source, total AS amount FROM orders WHERE status='paid' UNION ALL SELECT 'booking', (check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate FROM bookings ORDER BY source, amount;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: INTERSECT keeps values present in both results. EXCEPT keeps values in the first result but not the second.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Set operations express overlap and difference directly.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The default forms remove duplicates; ALL forms retain multiplicities according to the operation. INTERSECT binds more tightly than UNION and EXCEPT.

• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: INSERT adds rows. RETURNING exposes the values of the rows actually inserted.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A data-entry workflow needs to know what the database stored, including defaults and generated identifiers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: List target columns explicitly. VALUES supplies matching values; INSERT ... SELECT copies a query result.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
List target columns explicitly. VALUES supplies matching values; INSERT ... SELECT copies a query result.

• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• RETURNING exposes values from rows changed by the statement.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: UPDATE changes matching rows. Expressions can use the old values in each row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Stock adjustments, price changes, and status transitions are common business operations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SET assigns columns; WHERE limits rows; RETURNING inspects changed rows. Test the WHERE predicate with SELECT first.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
SET assigns columns; WHERE limits rows; RETURNING inspects changed rows. Test the WHERE predicate with SELECT first.

• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Set stock to 10 only for products currently at zero.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Set each product stock to the corresponding inventory quantity plus 2, leaving other columns unchanged.
sections.code: UPDATE products p SET stock=i.quantity+2 FROM inventory i WHERE i.product_id=p.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:

This table comes from the dedicated checker query that inspects the resulting state; it is separate from the command output shown when you run the example.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: An omitted WHERE changes every row. UPDATE ... FROM with multiple source matches can choose an unpredictable source row.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DELETE removes matching rows. Foreign-key actions decide whether dependent rows prevent or follow a deletion.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Retention and correction workflows must preserve referential integrity.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use DELETE FROM ... WHERE. DELETE ... USING can join supporting tables. TRUNCATE quickly empties whole tables with different locking and trigger behavior.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use DELETE FROM ... WHERE. DELETE ... USING can join supporting tables. TRUNCATE quickly empties whole tables with different locking and trigger behavior.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• DELETE FROM names the target; WHERE chooses which rows are removed.
sections.code: DELETE FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id);

sections.body: Deleting a parent row may fail when child rows exist. TRUNCATE is transactional in PostgreSQL but takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An upsert inserts a new row or updates an existing row when a unique constraint conflicts.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Idempotent import jobs can retry without creating duplicate primary keys.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE uses EXCLUDED to refer to the proposed new row. DO NOTHING skips a conflict.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE uses EXCLUDED to refer to the proposed new row. DO NOTHING skips a conflict.

• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
• ON CONFLICT selects the conflict key and merge action; EXCLUDED refers to proposed values.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES (1,'Central',60,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET warehouse=EXCLUDED.warehouse,quantity=EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Upsert product_id 1 in inventory with warehouse Central, quantity 60, updated_on 2024-08-01. Replace these values on conflict.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES (1,'Central',60,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET warehouse=EXCLUDED.warehouse,quantity=EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Upsert inventory row for product 2, warehouse North, quantity 5, date 2024-08-01. On conflict add 5 to existing quantity and update updated_on, preserving warehouse.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES(2,'North',5,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity=inventory.quantity+EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A transaction makes a sequence of changes succeed or fail as one unit. A savepoint marks a point that can be rolled back inside it.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A transfer must debit one account and credit another without exposing half a transfer.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BEGIN starts; COMMIT keeps changes; ROLLBACK discards them. SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT allow partial recovery. Each submitted practice run uses a fresh isolated database.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
BEGIN starts; COMMIT keeps changes; ROLLBACK discards them. SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT allow partial recovery. Each submitted practice run uses a fresh isolated database.

• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
• BEGIN opens a transaction; COMMIT keeps changes and ROLLBACK discards them.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Transfer 100 from account 1 to account 2 in one explicit transaction.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: In a transaction add 10 to account 1, create a savepoint, add another 100, roll back only the second addition, and commit.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+10 WHERE id=1; SAVEPOINT before_extra; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=1; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_extra; COMMIT;

This table comes from the dedicated checker query that inspects the resulting state; it is separate from the command output shown when you run the example.

1 | 900.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: After an error, a transaction is aborted until rolled back. Do not catch an error and continue as if earlier work committed.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A transaction makes a sequence of changes succeed or fail as one unit. A savepoint marks a point that can be rolled back inside it. BEGIN starts; COMMIT keeps changes; ROLLBACK discards them.

exercises.title: Transfer funds atomically
exercises.prompt: Transfer 100 from account 1 to account 2 in one explicit transaction.
exercises.solutionSQL: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;
hints: First identify the result grain: what does one output row represent in ‘Transfer funds atomically’?
BEGIN starts; COMMIT keeps changes; ROLLBACK discards them. SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT allow partial recovery. Each submitted practice run uses a fresh isolated database.
After an error, a transaction is aborted until rolled back. Do not catch an error and continue as if earlier work committed.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A data-changing CTE can use RETURNING rows as input to another operation in the same statement.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Moving rows into an audit table can be expressed with one statement and a clear data flow.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A modifying WITH query executes once. Its RETURNING output is the relation visible to the rest of the statement. Sibling statements share one snapshot.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
A modifying WITH query executes once. Its RETURNING output is the relation visible to the rest of the statement. Sibling statements share one snapshot.

• WITH gives a query stage a name; the final SELECT reads its output.
• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
• RETURNING exposes values from rows changed by the statement.
sections.code: WITH changed AS (UPDATE products SET price=price-1 WHERE category='Home' RETURNING id,price) SELECT id,price FROM changed ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Use an UPDATE CTE to reduce Home product prices by 1 and return id and new price, ordered by id.
sections.code: WITH changed AS (UPDATE products SET price=price-1 WHERE category='Home' RETURNING id,price) SELECT id,price FROM changed ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Insert product 51 named Eraser, Office category, price 1.25, stock 30 through a CTE, then return id and name.
sections.code: WITH added AS (INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES(51,'Eraser','Office',1.25,30) RETURNING id,name) SELECT id,name FROM added;

exercises.title: Archive deleted documents
exercises.prompt: Create document_archive(id integer PRIMARY KEY,title text). Move documents without SQL in body (case-insensitive) into the archive using DELETE RETURNING.
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE TABLE document_archive(id integer PRIMARY KEY,title text); WITH removed AS (DELETE FROM documents WHERE body !~* 'SQL' RETURNING id,title) INSERT INTO document_archive SELECT id,title FROM removed;
hints: First identify the result grain: what does one output row represent in ‘Archive deleted documents’?
A modifying WITH query executes once. Its RETURNING output is the relation visible to the rest of the statement. Sibling statements share one snapshot.
Do not rely on the physical execution order of sibling modifying CTEs or update the same row twice within one statement.
exercises.explanation: A data-changing CTE can use RETURNING rows as input to another operation in the same statement. A modifying WITH query executes once. Its RETURNING output is the relation visible to the rest of the statement. Sibling statements share one snapshot. The reference preserves the prompt’s output grain, NULL policy, and required order on both datasets. Different SQL is accepted when it satisfies those checks.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A data type defines which values a column accepts and which operations make sense. PostgreSQL has smallint, integer, bigint, numeric, text, and boolean types.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Choosing types prevents invalid data and makes calculations predictable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: INTEGER is exact within its range; NUMERIC stores exact decimals; TEXT stores variable-length text; BOOLEAN stores true, false, or NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
INTEGER is exact within its range; NUMERIC stores exact decimals; TEXT stores variable-length text; BOOLEAN stores true, false, or NULL.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
sections.code: SELECT pg_typeof(1)::text AS integer_type, pg_typeof(1.5)::text AS decimal_type, pg_typeof('x'::text)::text AS text_type, pg_typeof(true)::text AS boolean_type;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return integer_type, decimal_type, text_type, and boolean_type using pg_typeof on 1, 1.5, the text x, and true. Cast each pg_typeof result to text.
sections.code: SELECT pg_typeof(1)::text AS integer_type, pg_typeof(1.5)::text AS decimal_type, pg_typeof('x'::text)::text AS text_type, pg_typeof(true)::text AS boolean_type;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return id and label formed as product- followed by id as text, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id, 'product-' || id::text AS label FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A UUID is a 128-bit identifier. An enum is a type with a fixed ordered set of text labels.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Distributed identifiers and constrained business states can be represented with explicit database types.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use uuid literals for known identifiers. CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM defines labels; comparisons follow their declaration order. PostgreSQL 18 includes uuidv4() and uuidv7(), but generated values are nondeterministic.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use uuid literals for known identifiers. CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM defines labels; comparisons follow their declaration order. PostgreSQL 18 includes uuidv4() and uuidv7(), but generated values are nondeterministic.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
sections.code: SELECT '123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000'::uuid AS identifier;

sections.title: A small example

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: String functions transform or inspect text. Normalization means consistently representing values before matching or storing them.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: External data often contains unwanted spaces or inconsistent case.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: lower and upper change case; trim removes edge spaces; length counts characters; concat_ws joins known parts with a separator.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
lower and upper change case; trim removes edge spaces; length counts characters; concat_ws joins known parts with a separator.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id, lower(email) AS normalized_email FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id and normalized_email as lowercase email for customers with a known email, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id, lower(email) AS normalized_email FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return id, name, and name_length, ordered by longest name first and id ascending for ties.
sections.code: SELECT id,name,length(name) AS name_length FROM customers ORDER BY name_length DESC,id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE stores local date and time fields. TIMESTAMPTZ stores an instant and displays it in the session time zone.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: An instant needs an unambiguous interpretation when users live in different time zones.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AT TIME ZONE converts between a local timestamp and an instant using a named time zone. Prefer explicit zones in reports.

sections.title: Read the syntax

AT TIME ZONE converts between a local timestamp and an instant using a named time zone. Prefer explicit zones in reports.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.

• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An interval represents a duration with month, day, and sub-day components. date_trunc rounds a timestamp down to a calendar boundary.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Time-series reports need consistent daily or monthly buckets and explicit interval semantics.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Group on date_trunc for calendar periods. Subtract timestamps for elapsed intervals. Use fixed reference dates in reproducible tests.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Group on date_trunc for calendar periods. Subtract timestamps for elapsed intervals. Use fixed reference dates in reproducible tests.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return month_start as a date and revenue as sum of total, ordered by month_start.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A realistic use

sections.code: SELECT id,EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (occurred_at-TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 00:00:00'))/60 AS minutes_since_start FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A PostgreSQL array stores an ordered collection of values of one element type. Arrays normally use one-based indexes.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A modest collection such as product tags can be useful, while relationships with their own attributes often need a separate table.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ARRAY[...] constructs an array; = ANY(array) tests membership; @> tests containment; cardinality counts elements; unnest expands rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
ARRAY[...] constructs an array; = ANY(array) tests membership; @> tests containment; cardinality counts elements; unnest expands rows.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE 'usb'=ANY(tags) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id and name of products whose tags contain usb, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE 'usb'=ANY(tags) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Expand product tags and return tag and product_count, ordered by product_count descending then tag.
sections.code: SELECT t.tag,count(*) AS product_count FROM products p CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(p.tags) AS t(tag) GROUP BY t.tag ORDER BY product_count DESC,t.tag;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: JSON stores JSON text; JSONB stores a decomposed representation that supports efficient operations and indexing.

sections.title: Why it exists

sections.title: How it works

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: JSONB operators can test structure and create modified documents. jsonb_set returns a new document with a path changed.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Attribute filters and small document updates can happen in SQL without fetching and rewriting entire application objects.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: @> tests containment; ? tests a top-level key. jsonb_set takes a text-array path and a JSONB replacement value.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
@> tests containment; ? tests a top-level key. jsonb_set takes a text-array path and a JSONB replacement value.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Constraints are database-enforced rules. A primary key combines uniqueness and non-NULL; a foreign key requires a matching referenced key.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Rules must hold no matter which application writes data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Declare constraints in CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE. A UNIQUE constraint ordinarily permits multiple NULLs; NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes that in PostgreSQL 15 and later.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Declare constraints in CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE. A UNIQUE constraint ordinarily permits multiple NULLs; NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes that in PostgreSQL 15 and later.

• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• CREATE TABLE declares names, types, defaults, and constraints as a durable contract.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_notes(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),body text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO customer_notes VALUES(1,1,'Call after 5');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create customer_notes with id integer primary key, customer_id integer not null referencing customers(id), and body text not null. Insert (1,1,Call after 5).
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_notes(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),body text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO customer_notes VALUES(1,1,'Call after 5');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Create customer_alias(customer_id integer references customers(id), alias text unique nulls not distinct).
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_alias(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),alias text UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:

This table comes from the dedicated checker query that inspects the resulting state; it is separate from the command output shown when you run the example.

— | — | —
id | integer | NO

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A foreign key does not automatically create an index on the referencing columns. A nullable foreign key can represent an optional relationship.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: CHECK constrains a row expression. DEFAULT supplies a value for an omitted column. Referential actions define what happens when a referenced row changes.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Data rules such as positive quantities should be enforced at the place all writers share.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A CHECK passes when its expression is true or NULL, so combine it with NOT NULL when missing values are forbidden. ON DELETE CASCADE removes dependents.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
A CHECK passes when its expression is true or NULL, so combine it with NOT NULL when missing values are forbidden. ON DELETE CASCADE removes dependents.

• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• CREATE TABLE declares names, types, defaults, and constraints as a durable contract.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE reservations(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK(quantity>0)); INSERT INTO reservations(id) VALUES(1);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create reservations(id integer primary key, quantity integer not null default 1 check(quantity>0)), then insert only id=1.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE reservations(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK(quantity>0)); INSERT INTO reservations(id) VALUES(1);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Add products.promoted boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN promoted boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Dedicated verification result after running the small example on the Retail dataset, observed in PostgreSQL 18.6: 1 row(s), with up to eight shown. NULL marks a missing SQL value. This table comes from the dedicated checker query that inspects the resulting state; it is separate from the command output shown when you run the example.

id | quantity
— | —
1 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A CHECK cannot safely maintain cross-row totals. Defaults are applied on insertion; they do not retroactively fill existing rows.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An identity column obtains values from a sequence. A sequence generates numbers independently of ordinary row transaction rollback.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Automatic identifiers reduce coordination between concurrent writers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY rejects ordinary explicit values; BY DEFAULT allows them. RETURNING retrieves generated values.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY rejects ordinary explicit values; BY DEFAULT allows them. RETURNING retrieves generated values.

• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• CREATE TABLE declares names, types, defaults, and constraints as a durable contract.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A product name should be maintained once, rather than in every order line.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: First identify entities and candidate keys, then place each attribute with the key that determines it. A junction table often has a composite key.

sections.title: Read the syntax

First identify entities and candidate keys, then place each attribute with the key that determines it. A junction table often has a composite key.

• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• CREATE TABLE declares names, types, defaults, and constraints as a durable contract.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE favorites(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),product_id integer REFERENCES products(id),PRIMARY KEY(customer_id,product_id)); INSERT INTO favorites VALUES(1,3),(2,1);

exercises.prompt: Return category, product_count, and repeated_name_copies (count minus one) for each product category. Order by category. This quantifies repeated category-name storage before normalization.

exercises.title: Relationship participation
exercises.prompt: Return every customer id as customer_id and the number of distinct products in their paid orders as distinct_products, including zero. Order by customer_id.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,count(DISTINCT i.product_id) AS distinct_products FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;
hints: Identify the entity represented by one output row.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A schema groups database objects in a namespace. System catalogs describe the database itself.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Namespaces avoid collisions; metadata makes tools and migrations inspectable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Unqualified names are resolved through search_path. information_schema offers portable metadata, while pg_catalog exposes PostgreSQL details.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Unqualified names are resolved through search_path. information_schema offers portable metadata, while pg_catalog exposes PostgreSQL details.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT column_name,data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_name='customers' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return column_name and data_type for customers in the current schema, ordered by ordinal_position.
sections.code: SELECT column_name,data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_name='customers' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return table_name for base tables in the current schema, ordered alphabetically.
sections.code: SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_type='BASE TABLE' ORDER BY table_name;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A migration is a versioned change to database structure or data. A reliable migration preserves intended facts and can be verified.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Applications evolve; ad hoc manual edits are hard to reproduce or review.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use explicit ALTER statements, backfill data, then add stronger constraints. Many PostgreSQL DDL operations are transactional, but locks and operation-specific restrictions still matter.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use explicit ALTER statements, backfill data, then add stronger constraints. Many PostgreSQL DDL operations are transactional, but locks and operation-specific restrictions still matter.

• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
• ALTER TABLE changes the contract of an existing table; its locks and existing data must be considered.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN segment text; UPDATE customers SET segment=CASE WHEN vip THEN 'priority' ELSE 'standard' END; ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN segment SET NOT NULL;

sections.title: A realistic use

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A window function calculates over rows related to the current row while keeping each detail row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: You can show each employee beside a department benchmark without collapsing employees into groups.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OVER defines a window. PARTITION BY divides rows into independent sets. An aggregate with OVER becomes a window calculation.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
OVER defines a window. PARTITION BY divides rows into independent sets. An aggregate with OVER becomes a window calculation.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• OVER defines the partition, order, and optional frame for a window calculation.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,department,salary,sum(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) AS department_total FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id, department, salary, and department_total as a window sum of salary by department, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id,department,salary,sum(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) AS department_total FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return id, customer_id, and customer_order_count as a window count by customer_id, ordered by id. Include the NULL customer partition.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,count(*) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_order_count FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results

Query result for the small example on the Retail dataset, observed in PostgreSQL 18.6: 6 row(s), with up to eight shown. NULL marks a missing SQL value.

id | department | salary | department_total

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: GROUP BY reduces rows; a window usually preserves them. Window functions run after WHERE and grouping and cannot be filtered directly in WHERE.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: ROW_NUMBER numbers rows; RANK gives equal values equal rank with gaps; DENSE_RANK gives equal ranks without gaps.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Leaderboards and top-N-per-group reports need an explicit policy for ties.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Place ordering inside OVER. Add a unique tie-breaker to ROW_NUMBER, but omit it from a ranking definition when equal measures should tie.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Place ordering inside OVER. Add a unique tie-breaker to ROW_NUMBER, but omit it from a ranking definition when equal measures should tie.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.

• OVER defines the partition, order, and optional frame for a window calculation.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,category,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS position FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example

sections.body: LAG reads a preceding row; LEAD reads a following row in window order.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Comparisons to a previous event or order do not require a self join.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The default offset is one. An optional default value applies when the requested row is outside the partition. PostgreSQL uses RESPECT NULLS behavior.

sections.title: Read the syntax

The default offset is one. An optional default value applies when the requested row is outside the partition. PostgreSQL uses RESPECT NULLS behavior.

sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,total,lag(total) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) AS previous_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A window frame selects a subset of the ordered partition for each current row. ROWS uses physical row positions; RANGE groups peers by ordering values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Cumulative and moving metrics need clear boundaries, especially when dates repeat.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW produces a deterministic running total when the window has unique ordering.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW produces a deterministic running total when the window has unique ordering.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• OVER defines the partition, order, and optional frame for a window calculation.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on,sum(total) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' ORDER BY ordered_on,id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id, ordered_on, and running_revenue for paid orders ordered by ordered_on then id; use an explicit ROWS frame and output in that order.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE read frame endpoints. NTILE assigns ordered rows to a chosen number of buckets.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Analytical reports often need a baseline, an end-of-period value, or approximately equal-size segments.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use an explicit frame through UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING when LAST_VALUE should see the end of the partition. NTILE divides rows, not value ranges.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use an explicit frame through UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING when LAST_VALUE should see the end of the partition. NTILE divides rows, not value ranges.

• OVER defines the partition, order, and optional frame for a window calculation.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON keeps the first row for each set of key expressions. It is a PostgreSQL-specific alternative to some ranking queries.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Selecting one latest record per customer is common in operational reports.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DISTINCT ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions. Additional sort keys decide which row is kept.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
DISTINCT ON expressions must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions. Additional sort keys decide which row is kept.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
CREATE VIEW name AS query defines it. A later query can filter or aggregate the view. Privilege behavior needs deliberate design for shared production use.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A materialized view stores a query result until it is refreshed.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Expensive read-heavy summaries can trade freshness for faster repeated access.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW stores initial rows. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW recomputes them. Concurrent refresh requires a qualifying unique index and an already-populated view.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW stores initial rows. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW recomputes them. Concurrent refresh requires a qualifying unique index and an already-populated view.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW stores query rows; REFRESH recomputes them.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A set-returning function supplies rows as a relation. generate_series creates sequences of numbers or time values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Calendar reports need dates with no events as well as dates that appear in the data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use FROM generate_series(...) AS alias(column). LEFT JOIN facts to a generated calendar and count a non-NULL fact key.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use FROM generate_series(...) AS alias(column). LEFT JOIN facts to a generated calendar and count a non-NULL fact key.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT n FROM generate_series(1,5) AS s(n) ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return n from 1 through 5 inclusive, ordered by n.
sections.code: SELECT n FROM generate_series(1,5) AS s(n) ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return booking_id and night for every occupied booking night (check-in inclusive, check-out exclusive), ordered by booking_id then night.
sections.code: SELECT b.id AS booking_id,n.day::date AS night FROM bookings b CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(b.check_in,b.check_out-1,INTERVAL '1 day') n(day) ORDER BY b.id,night;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A SQL function packages a calculation or query behind a typed interface. Volatility describes how results may change.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reusable business calculations benefit from explicit argument and result types.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE FUNCTION lists arguments, RETURNS type, LANGUAGE sql, and a body. IMMUTABLE promises equal inputs always yield equal outputs; STABLE allows database reads within a statement snapshot.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
CREATE FUNCTION lists arguments, RETURNS type, LANGUAGE sql, and a body. IMMUTABLE promises equal inputs always yield equal outputs; STABLE allows database reads within a statement snapshot.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• CREATE FUNCTION declares argument types, return type, language, and a body between dollar-quote delimiters.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION add_vat(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*1.20,2) $$;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create add_vat(amount numeric) returning numeric, LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE, multiplying amount by 1.20 and rounding to two decimals.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION add_vat(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*1.20,2) $$;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Complete product_label(pid integer) returning text to return the product name for the supplied ID; LANGUAGE sql STABLE.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION product_label(pid integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$ SELECT name FROM products WHERE id=pid $$;

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A wrong IMMUTABLE label can produce incorrect optimized results. Avoid SECURITY DEFINER unless you deliberately need and secure its elevated privileges.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A SQL function packages a calculation or query behind a typed interface. Volatility describes how results may change. CREATE FUNCTION lists arguments, RETURNS type, LANGUAGE sql, and a body.

exercises.title: Create a VAT calculation
exercises.prompt: Create add_vat(amount numeric) returning numeric, LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE, multiplying amount by 1.20 and rounding to two decimals.
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE FUNCTION add_vat(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*1.20,2) $$;

exercises.title: An exact immutable discount function
exercises.prompt: Create discounted_price(amount numeric, percent numeric) returning numeric as a SQL IMMUTABLE STRICT function. Return amount*(1-percent/100), rounded to two decimals.
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE FUNCTION discounted_price(amount numeric,percent numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE STRICT AS $$ SELECT round(amount*(1-percent/100),2) $$;
hints: Divide the percentage by 100 using numeric arithmetic.
Use round(...,2) on the final amount.
Declare and verify both IMMUTABLE and STRICT.
exercises.explanation: Exact numeric arithmetic avoids floating-point money errors. STRICT returns NULL without executing the body for NULL input; volatility is part of the function contract.

exercises.title: A stable paid-total function
exercises.prompt: Create customer_paid_total(cid integer) returning numeric as a SQL STABLE function. Sum total for that customer’s paid orders; return zero if none exist.
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE FUNCTION customer_paid_total(cid integer) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$ SELECT COALESCE(sum(total),0) FROM orders WHERE customer_id=cid AND status='paid' $$;
hints: Aggregate only paid rows for the argument customer.
SUM on no rows is NULL.
A table-reading function should not be labeled IMMUTABLE.
exercises.explanation: The result depends on tables, so it is not immutable. STABLE describes consistency within a statement snapshot, while COALESCE implements the zero-result policy.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PL/pgSQL adds variables, branches, loops, and exception handling to SQL functions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Some server-side rules need several dependent decisions rather than one SQL expression.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A dollar-quoted body commonly contains DECLARE, BEGIN, statements, RETURN, and END. Assignment uses := and IF ends with END IF.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
A dollar-quoted body commonly contains DECLARE, BEGIN, statements, RETURN, and END. Assignment uses := and IF ends with END IF.

• CREATE FUNCTION declares argument types, return type, language, and a body between dollar-quote delimiters.
• BEGIN opens a transaction; COMMIT keeps changes and ROLLBACK discards them.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION stock_label(qty integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$ BEGIN IF qty=0 THEN RETURN 'empty'; ELSIF qty<10 THEN RETURN 'low'; ELSE RETURN 'ready'; END IF; END $$;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create stock_label(qty integer) returning text in PL/pgSQL: empty for 0, low for values below 10, otherwise ready.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION stock_label(qty integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$ BEGIN IF qty=0 THEN RETURN 'empty'; ELSIF qty<10 THEN RETURN 'low'; ELSE RETURN 'ready'; END IF; END $$;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Create booking_charge(bid integer) returning numeric in PL/pgSQL. Read nights times nightly_rate for that booking into a local variable and return it.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION booking_charge(bid integer) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$ DECLARE charge numeric; BEGIN SELECT (check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate INTO charge FROM bookings WHERE id=bid; RETURN charge; END $$;

exercises.title: Loop through a fixed stock adjustment
exercises.prompt: Create PL/pgSQL IMMUTABLE function triangular_stock(n integer) returning integer. Use a loop to sum integers 1 through n; return 0 for n<1.

Return the accumulated value after the loop ends.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A procedure is invoked with CALL and can perform operations without being used as a value expression.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A named server-side operation can define a controlled multi-step business action.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE PROCEDURE declares arguments and a body. A function returns a value; a procedure has distinct invocation and transaction-control rules.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
CREATE PROCEDURE declares arguments and a body. A function returns a value; a procedure has distinct invocation and transaction-control rules.

• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
• CREATE PROCEDURE declares a named operation; CALL invokes it.
• BEGIN opens a transaction; COMMIT keeps changes and ROLLBACK discards them.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE restock(pid integer,units integer) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock=stock+units WHERE id=pid; END $$; CALL restock(1,7);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create restock(pid integer,units integer) in PL/pgSQL that adds units to products.stock for pid; call it for product 1 with 7 units.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE restock(pid integer,units integer) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock=stock+units WHERE id=pid; END $$; CALL restock(1,7);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Create mark_inventory_checked(as_of date) in PL/pgSQL setting every inventory.updated_on to as_of. Call it with 2024-08-15.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE mark_inventory_checked(as_of date) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE inventory SET updated_on=as_of; END $$; CALL mark_inventory_checked(DATE '2024-08-15');
