sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Transaction control inside a procedure is permitted only in specific top-level CALL contexts. The practice procedures leave transaction boundaries to their caller.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A trigger automatically runs a function in response to a table event. A row trigger sees NEW and/or OLD records.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Auditing or invariant maintenance sometimes must happen for every writer.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE TRIGGER names timing, event, target table, row or statement scope, and the trigger function. BEFORE row triggers may modify and return NEW.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
CREATE TRIGGER names timing, event, target table, row or statement scope, and the trigger function. BEFORE row triggers may modify and return NEW.

• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• CREATE FUNCTION declares argument types, return type, language, and a body between dollar-quote delimiters.
• CREATE TRIGGER states timing, event, row/statement scope, and the trigger function.
• BEGIN opens a transaction; COMMIT keeps changes and ROLLBACK discards them.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION trim_customer_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER normalize_name BEFORE INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION trim_customer_name(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(60,'  Zara  ',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create a BEFORE INSERT row trigger on customers that trims NEW.name. Insert customer 60 with name surrounded by two spaces (Zara), joined_on 2024-08-01.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION trim_customer_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER normalize_name BEFORE INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION trim_customer_name(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(60,'  Zara  ',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Create a BEFORE INSERT row trigger on products rounding NEW.price to one decimal place. Insert product 60, Clip, Office, 1.26, stock 5.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION round_product_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.price:=round(NEW.price,1); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER product_round BEFORE INSERT ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION round_product_price(); INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES(60,'Clip','Office',1.26,5);

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Hidden trigger work can surprise callers. A trigger that recursively updates its own table needs careful control.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE FUNCTION round_product_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.price:=round(NEW.price,1); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER product_round BEFORE INSERT ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION round_product_price(); INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES(60,'Clip','Office',1.26,5);
hints: First identify the result grain: what does one output row represent in ‘Round inserted product prices’?
CREATE TRIGGER names timing, event, target table, row or statement scope, and the trigger function. BEFORE row triggers may modify and return NEW.
Hidden trigger work can surprise callers. A trigger that recursively updates its own table needs careful control.
exercises.explanation: A trigger automatically runs a function in response to a table event. A row trigger sees NEW and/or OLD records. CREATE TRIGGER names timing, event, target table, row or statement scope, and the trigger function. BEFORE row triggers may modify and return NEW. exercises.title: Normalize a newly assigned customer email
exercises.prompt: Create a BEFORE UPDATE OF email row trigger on customers, named clean_email, that sets NEW.email to lower(trim(NEW.email)). Use a PL/pgSQL trigger function named normalize_email. Then set customer 1 email to two spaces + ADA.NEW@EXAMPLE.TEST + two spaces.
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE FUNCTION normalize_email() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.email:=lower(trim(NEW.email)); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER clean_email BEFORE UPDATE OF email ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION normalize_email(); UPDATE customers SET email='  ADA.NEW@EXAMPLE.TEST  ' WHERE id=1;
hints: The trigger must run before the row is stored.
Assign the normalized value to NEW.email.
Return NEW so PostgreSQL continues the update.
exercises.explanation: A BEFORE trigger can replace NEW before constraints are checked. RETURN NEW keeps the updated row rather than suppressing it.

exercises.title: Fill an omitted event device
exercises.prompt: Create trigger fill_event_device BEFORE INSERT on events using PL/pgSQL function default_event_device(). When NEW.payload lacks the device key, add device=unknown without removing existing keys. Insert event (id 60, customer_id 1, occurred_at 2024-08-01 12:00, kind visit, payload {"pages":2}).
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE FUNCTION default_event_device() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF NOT (NEW.payload ? 'device') THEN NEW.payload:=NEW.payload||'{"device":"unknown"}'::jsonb; END IF; RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER fill_event_device BEFORE INSERT ON events FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION default_event_device(); INSERT INTO events VALUES(60,1,TIMESTAMP '2024-08-01 12:00','visit','{"pages":2}');
hints: Use the JSONB key-existence operator ?.
Only add the default when the key is absent.
Return the modified NEW row.
exercises.explanation: The existence operator distinguishes a missing key from an existing key. JSONB concatenation adds the default while retaining unrelated data.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An audit trigger records facts about a change, including the prior and new values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A history table helps explain how important business data changed.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For UPDATE, OLD contains the previous row and NEW contains the proposed or stored row depending on timing. An AFTER trigger normally returns NULL because its return value is ignored.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
For UPDATE, OLD contains the previous row and NEW contains the proposed or stored row depending on timing. An AFTER trigger normally returns NULL because its return value is ignored.

• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
• CREATE TABLE declares names, types, defaults, and constraints as a durable contract.
• CREATE FUNCTION declares argument types, return type, language, and a body between dollar-quote delimiters.
• CREATE TRIGGER states timing, event, row/statement scope, and the trigger function.
• BEGIN opens a transaction; COMMIT keeps changes and ROLLBACK discards them.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric,new_price numeric); CREATE FUNCTION audit_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO price_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_price(); UPDATE products SET price=price+2 WHERE id=1;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric,new_price numeric), an AFTER UPDATE OF price row trigger on products recording OLD and NEW prices, then add 2 to product 1 price.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric,new_price numeric); CREATE FUNCTION audit_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO price_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_price(); UPDATE products SET price=price+2 WHERE id=1;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Create customer_audit(customer_id integer,name text), an AFTER INSERT row trigger on customers that copies id and name, then insert customer 61, Yara, joined_on 2024-08-01.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_audit(customer_id integer,name text); CREATE FUNCTION audit_customer_insert() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO customer_audit VALUES(NEW.id,NEW.name); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER customer_insertion AFTER INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_customer_insert(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(61,'Yara',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Avoid auditing every column without a retention policy. Audit tables need their own permissions and integrity guarantees in production.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Full-text search converts documents into searchable lexemes and evaluates structured search queries.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Word-aware search handles stemming and stop words better than simple substring matching.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: to_tsvector creates a document representation; plainto_tsquery parses ordinary search words; @@ tests a match. Choose an explicit configuration such as english.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
to_tsvector creates a document representation; plainto_tsquery parses ordinary search words; @@ tests a match. Choose an explicit configuration such as english.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english','SQL') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id and title for documents matching the English full-text search SQL, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english','SQL') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use

sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ phraseto_tsquery('english','SQL queries') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An index is an auxiliary data structure that can locate rows without scanning every table row. B-tree supports equality and ordered range lookups; Hash supports equality.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Selective lookups and ordered retrieval can become much faster, at the cost of space and write work.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE INDEX names a table and key expressions. The planner chooses whether an index is worth using based on estimated costs and selectivity.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
CREATE INDEX names a table and key expressions. The planner chooses whether an index is worth using based on estimated costs and selectivity.

• CREATE INDEX declares the access method and key expressions; a partial predicate limits indexed rows.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_date ON orders USING btree(customer_id,ordered_on);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create a B-tree index named orders_customer_date on orders(customer_id,ordered_on).
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_date ON orders USING btree(customer_id,ordered_on);

sections.title: A realistic use

sections.code: SELECT count(*) FILTER(WHERE price<20) AS matching_rows,count(*) AS total_rows FROM products;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: GIN indexes components of compound values; GiST is a framework for strategies such as range overlap; BRIN summarizes block ranges.

sections.title: Why it exists

sections.title: How it works

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A partial index covers rows satisfying a predicate. An expression index stores computed keys. INCLUDE adds non-key payload columns.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A workload may repeatedly query only pending orders or normalized email values.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The query predicate must imply the partial index predicate for use. Indexed functions must be immutable. INCLUDE can support index-only scans when visibility information permits.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
The query predicate must imply the partial index predicate for use. Indexed functions must be immutable. INCLUDE can support index-only scans when visibility information permits.

• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• CREATE INDEX declares the access method and key expressions; a partial predicate limits indexed rows.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_pending_date ON orders(ordered_on) WHERE status='pending';

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Create orders_pending_date on orders(ordered_on) only where status is pending.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_pending_date ON orders(ordered_on) WHERE status='pending';

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Create orders_customer_cover on orders(customer_id) INCLUDE(total,ordered_on).
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_cover ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE(total,ordered_on);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Dedicated verification result after running the small example on the Retail dataset, observed in PostgreSQL 18.6: 1 row(s), with up to eight shown. NULL marks a missing SQL value. This table comes from the dedicated checker query that inspects the resulting state; it is separate from the command output shown when you run the example.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Wrapping an indexed column in a different expression may prevent a matching access path. Extra included columns make the index larger.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prerequisites: Tables, rows, and basic expressions. Compare the small example with the realistic task: the concept stays the same when more rows are added.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Complete the 5 exercises in order. Run a draft, inspect its rows, then submit. A wrong result does not erase your progress. Use one hint at a time. If you need the worked solution, return to the exercise later and try it again. Revisit your attempts in the Learning Center to understand mistakes.

sections.title: Why it exists

sections.body: Optimization preserves a query result while reducing unnecessary work. The correct grain, predicates, and join structure matter before index changes.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A faster wrong report is still wrong. Alternative SQL is valuable when its meaning is established.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Filter early when semantics permit, select only needed columns, and avoid repeated work. Compare actual plans on representative data.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Filter early when semantics permit, select only needed columns, and avoid repeated work. Compare actual plans on representative data.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PostgreSQL keeps old row versions for concurrent readers. VACUUM reclaims reusable space and maintains visibility information; ANALYZE updates statistics.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Updates and deletes do not immediately remove every old row version. Regular maintenance keeps a changing database healthy.

sections.title: How it works

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A performance investigation separates query meaning, estimated work, actual work, and system conditions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Changing random settings can mask a problem while creating another one.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Record the slow query and workload, inspect EXPLAIN, compare estimates with actual rows, check indexes and statistics, then measure a targeted change.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Record the slow query and workload, inspect EXPLAIN, compare estimates with actual rows, check indexes and statistics, then measure a targeted change.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

exercises.title: Explain two reads and one concurrent commit
exercises.prompt: A transaction reads an account balance. Another transaction commits a new balance. The first transaction reads the balance again. Explain the possible result under READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ, and explain why a SERIALIZABLE application still needs retry logic. This written answer is self-assessed against a model explanation.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT true AS discussed;
hints: Separate a statement snapshot from a transaction snapshot.
Consider whether the second SELECT obtains a new snapshot.
Distinguish isolation guarantees from a promise that every transaction will commit.
exercises.explanation: Read your answer against the model, identify missing points, and mark it reviewed when you can explain the distinction in your own words.
exercises.modelAnswer: Under READ COMMITTED, each statement obtains a new snapshot. The second SELECT can see the newly committed balance. Under REPEATABLE READ, both reads use the transaction snapshot, so a newly committed external change is not visible to the second read. SERIALIZABLE adds protection against serialization anomalies, but PostgreSQL can abort a transaction with a serialization failure. The application must retry the entire transaction, with bounded retry policy and no duplicated external side effects.

lessons.title: Row locks, NOWAIT, and SKIP LOCKED

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A row lock coordinates writers working on the same row. NOWAIT errors instead of waiting; SKIP LOCKED omits locked rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Transfers and worker queues need explicit concurrency rules.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks selected rows until transaction end. Lock rows in a consistent order. The current workspace runs one learner operation at a time, so it cannot demonstrate an actual competing waiter.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks selected rows until transaction end. Lock rows in a consistent order. The current workspace runs one learner operation at a time, so it cannot demonstrate an actual competing waiter.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
sections.code: SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait in a cycle. A connection pool reuses database sessions to control connection overhead.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reliable applications retry transient failures and avoid overwhelming the server with unbounded connections.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use consistent lock order and short transactions. Retry a whole transaction after deadlock or serialization failure using bounded backoff. Transaction pooling does not preserve arbitrary session state between transactions.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use consistent lock order and short transactions. Retry a whole transaction after deadlock or serialization failure using bounded backoff. Transaction pooling does not preserve arbitrary session state between transactions.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• UPDATE names the target table; SET defines new values and WHERE limits affected rows.
• BEGIN opens a transaction; COMMIT keeps changes and ROLLBACK discards them.
sections.code: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-15 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+15 WHERE id=3; COMMIT;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: In one explicit transaction, lock account 1 then account 3 by selecting each FOR UPDATE, transfer 15 from 1 to 3, and commit.
sections.code: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-15 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+15 WHERE id=3; COMMIT;

sections.body: Transfer 20 from account 1 to 2 in one transaction, changing only those accounts and preserving the total balance.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A deadlock occurs when transactions wait in a cycle. A connection pool reuses database sessions to control connection overhead. Use consistent lock order and short transactions.

exercises.title: Use consistent lock order
exercises.prompt: In one explicit transaction, lock account 1 then account 3 by selecting each FOR UPDATE, transfer 15 from 1 to 3, and commit.
exercises.solutionSQL: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-15 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+15 WHERE id=3; COMMIT;
hints: First identify the result grain: what does one output row represent in ‘Use consistent lock order’?

Use consistent lock order and short transactions. Retry a whole transaction after deadlock or serialization failure using bounded backoff. Transaction pooling does not preserve arbitrary session state between transactions.
Do not retry only the last failed statement of an aborted transaction. Temporary tables and session-level settings may not survive transaction pooling as expected.

exercises.title: Make a retried debit idempotent
exercises.prompt: Create debit_requests(id integer PRIMARY KEY, account_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id), amount numeric NOT NULL CHECK(amount>0)). Apply request (1,1,30) twice; debit account 1 exactly once by using INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING to gate each UPDATE.
exercises.solutionSQL: CREATE TABLE debit_requests(id integer PRIMARY KEY,account_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),amount numeric NOT NULL CHECK(amount>0)); WITH accepted AS (INSERT INTO debit_requests VALUES(1,1,30) ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING RETURNING account_id,amount) UPDATE accounts a SET balance=a.balance-x.amount FROM accepted x WHERE a.id=x.account_id; WITH accepted AS (INSERT INTO debit_requests VALUES(1,1,30) ON CONFLICT(id) DO NOTHING RETURNING account_id,amount) UPDATE accounts a SET balance=a.balance-x.amount FROM accepted x WHERE a.id=x.account_id;
hints: Use a persistent unique request key.
A conflicting DO NOTHING insert returns no row.
Update only accounts matched to the accepted rows.
exercises.explanation: A unique request identifier detects repetition. The data-changing CTE returns a row only for the first accepted request, preventing the second debit.

exercises.title: Verify transaction-local cleanup
exercises.prompt: Set LOCAL application_name to temporary_task inside a transaction, commit, then return one Boolean column restored indicating that the session application_name is no longer temporary_task.
exercises.solutionSQL: BEGIN; SET LOCAL application_name='temporary_task'; COMMIT; SELECT current_setting('application_name')<>'temporary_task' AS restored;
hints: Use SET LOCAL rather than a session-wide SET.
COMMIT before the inspection SELECT.
Return a comparison result, not a hardcoded application name.
exercises.explanation: SET LOCAL lasts only until the transaction ends. This avoids leaking request-specific state when a connection is reused.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A role is a database identity that can own objects and receive privileges. A login role can open sessions; a group role can collect permissions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Applications should have only the capabilities their work requires.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GRANT gives privileges and REVOKE removes them. Object ownership includes powerful management rights. The practice role is deliberately not a superuser, role creator, or database creator.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
GRANT gives privileges and REVOKE removes them. Object ownership includes powerful management rights. The practice role is deliberately not a superuser, role creator, or database creator.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
sections.code: SELECT has_table_privilege(current_user,'products','SELECT') AS can_select;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return can_select containing whether current_user has SELECT privilege on products.
sections.code: SELECT has_table_privilege(current_user,'products','SELECT') AS can_select;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Revoke ALL privileges on products from PUBLIC, preserving the current owner access.
sections.code: REVOKE ALL ON products FROM PUBLIC;

exercises.title: Inspect schema privileges
exercises.prompt: Return schema_usage and schema_create indicating whether current_user has USAGE and CREATE on the public schema.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT has_schema_privilege(current_user,'public','USAGE') AS schema_usage,has_schema_privilege(current_user,'public','CREATE') AS schema_create;
hints: Inspect the current role rather than guessing its name.
Schema privileges and role attributes are different security layers.

sections.body: SQL injection happens when untrusted text is treated as SQL syntax. A parameterized query sends values separately from command structure.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A name containing a quote must remain data rather than changing the meaning of a query.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PostgreSQL prepared statements use $1, $2, and typed parameters. Client libraries provide binding APIs. SQL identifiers need separate safe composition rules; they cannot be bound as ordinary value parameters.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
PostgreSQL prepared statements use $1, $2, and typed parameters. Client libraries provide binding APIs. SQL identifiers need separate safe composition rules; they cannot be bound as ordinary value parameters.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
• PREPARE declares a command with typed placeholders such as $1. EXECUTE supplies values separately.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Row-level security, or RLS, adds per-row access rules after ordinary table privileges.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Multi-tenant or restricted data views may need row rules enforced in the database.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY activates policies. CREATE POLICY defines USING for visible rows and WITH CHECK for proposed rows. Owners normally bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY activates policies. CREATE POLICY defines USING for visible rows and WITH CHECK for proposed rows. Owners normally bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
• ALTER TABLE changes the contract of an existing table; its locks and existing data must be considered.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE customers FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY vip_only ON customers FOR SELECT USING(vip); SELECT id,name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A backup is a recoverable copy of data and the information needed to restore it. A copy of query rows alone is not a complete database backup.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Recovery must be tested before an accident, including schema, constraints, roles, and expected application behavior.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: pg_dump makes a logical database backup; pg_restore reads archive formats. A production process also plans globals, retention, encryption, and point-in-time recovery. CLI backup tools are covered conceptually; this query workspace does not execute host commands.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
pg_dump makes a logical database backup; pg_restore reads archive formats. A production process also plans globals, retention, encryption, and point-in-time recovery. CLI backup tools are covered conceptually; this query workspace does not execute host commands.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• CREATE TABLE declares names, types, defaults, and constraints as a durable contract.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Operational troubleshooting connects symptoms to evidence from the database, application, and host.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A recursive CTE starts with anchor rows and repeatedly applies a recursive term until no new rows remain.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Trees and graph paths have an unknown number of levels, which a fixed number of joins cannot express.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: WITH RECURSIVE names the CTE. UNION ALL combines the anchor and recursive term. The recursive term joins the current working set to the next links.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
WITH RECURSIVE names the CTE. UNION ALL combines the anchor and recursive term. The recursive term joins the current working set to the next links.

• WITH RECURSIVE names the anchor and recursive working relation. The recursive term reads the prior working rows.
• WITH gives a query stage a name; the final SELECT reads its output.
• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return n from 1 through 5 using a recursive CTE, ordered by n.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return id and name of all direct and indirect reports of employee 2, excluding employee 2, ordered by id.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (SELECT id,name FROM employees WHERE manager_id=2 UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.name FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id=r.id) SELECT id,name FROM reports ORDER BY id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A path records visited identifiers during recursion. It can support breadcrumbs and prevent revisiting a node.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Real graph data can contain cycles even when a business process expects a tree.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Append each new ID to an array and reject IDs already in the path. PostgreSQL also provides SEARCH and CYCLE clauses for recursive queries.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Append each new ID to an array and reject IDs already in the path. PostgreSQL also provides SEARCH and CYCLE clauses for recursive queries.

• WITH RECURSIVE names the anchor and recursive working relation. The recursive term reads the prior working rows.
• WITH gives a query stage a name; the final SELECT reads its output.
• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (SELECT id,manager_id,ARRAY[id] AS path FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.manager_id,t.path||e.id FROM employees e JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id=t.id WHERE NOT e.id=ANY(t.path)) SELECT id,path FROM tree ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id and path as an integer array from root to employee, ordered by id.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (SELECT id,manager_id,ARRAY[id] AS path FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.manager_id,t.path||e.id FROM employees e JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id=t.id WHERE NOT e.id=ANY(t.path)) SELECT id,path FROM tree ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Use edges (1,2),(2,3),(3,1),(2,4), start node 1, and return distinct reachable node IDs including 1 as node, ordered by node. Prevent infinite recursion.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE edges(a,b) AS (VALUES(1,2),(2,3),(3,1),(2,4)), walk(node) AS (SELECT 1 UNION SELECT e.b FROM walk w JOIN edges e ON e.a=w.node) SELECT node FROM walk ORDER BY node;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A recursive traversal can connect each ancestor with all descendants before aggregation.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Managers may need totals for their complete reporting subtree, not just direct reports.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Keep the ancestor ID fixed while recursively following children. Aggregate at the ancestor grain after traversal.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Keep the ancestor ID fixed while recursively following children. Aggregate at the ancestor grain after traversal.

• WITH RECURSIVE names the anchor and recursive working relation. The recursive term reads the prior working rows.
• WITH gives a query stage a name; the final SELECT reads its output.
• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE links AS (SELECT id AS manager_id,id AS employee_id FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT l.manager_id,e.id FROM links l JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id=l.employee_id) SELECT manager_id,count(*)-1 AS report_count FROM links GROUP BY manager_id ORDER BY manager_id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return manager_id and report_count for every employee, excluding themselves from their own report count, ordered by manager_id.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE links AS (SELECT id AS manager_id,id AS employee_id FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT l.manager_id,e.id FROM links l JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id=l.employee_id) SELECT manager_id,count(*)-1 AS report_count FROM links GROUP BY manager_id ORDER BY manager_id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return id and name for employees with no direct reports, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT e.id,e.name FROM employees e WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM employees child WHERE child.manager_id=e.id) ORDER BY e.id;

exercises.prompt: For every employee treated as a possible leader, return leader_id and maximum_depth of that employee’s reporting subtree. Include the leader at depth 0. Order by leader_id.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH RECURSIVE links AS (SELECT id AS leader_id,id AS employee_id,0 AS depth FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT l.leader_id,e.id,l.depth+1 FROM links l JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id=l.employee_id) SELECT leader_id,max(depth) AS maximum_depth FROM links GROUP BY leader_id ORDER BY leader_id;

Leaf detection uses the absence of a child relationship.
exercises.explanation: Anchoring every employee generates one traversal per possible leader. MAX(depth) summarizes the deepest reporting chain without counting paths as employees.

exercises.title: Salary budget for leaf reports
exercises.prompt: For each employee treated as a leader, return leader_id and leaf_salary: the sum of salary for leaf employees in that subtree, including the leader if they are a leaf. Order by leader_id.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH RECURSIVE links AS (SELECT id AS leader_id,id AS employee_id FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT l.leader_id,e.id FROM links l JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id=l.employee_id) SELECT l.leader_id,sum(e.salary) AS leaf_salary FROM links l JOIN employees e ON e.id=l.employee_id WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM employees child WHERE child.manager_id=e.id) GROUP BY l.leader_id ORDER BY l.leader_id;
hints: Separate recursive membership from the final aggregate.
Decide explicitly whether the leader contributes to the measure.
Leaf detection uses the absence of a child relationship.
exercises.explanation: A leaf has no children. Generate ancestor-descendant membership first, then restrict the contributing employees before summing their salaries.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A range value represents a set of ordered values with explicit inclusive or exclusive bounds. PostgreSQL has built-in date, timestamp, and numeric ranges.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Booking and scheduling rules are clearer when overlap is one typed operation.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: daterange(start,end,'[)') includes check-in and excludes check-out. The && operator tests overlap; @> tests containment.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
daterange(start,end,'[)') includes check-in and excludes check-out. The && operator tests overlap; @> tests containment.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest FROM bookings WHERE daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)') @> DATE '2024-07-03' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id and guest for bookings whose half-open date range contains 2024-07-03, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest FROM bookings WHERE daterange(check_in,check_out,'[)') @> DATE '2024-07-03' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return first_booking and second_booking IDs for overlapping bookings in the same room, each pair once with first ID smaller, ordered by both IDs.
sections.code: SELECT a.id AS first_booking,b.id AS second_booking FROM bookings a JOIN bookings b ON a.room=b.room AND a.id<b.id AND daterange(a.check_in,a.check_out,'[)') && daterange(b.check_in,b.check_out,'[)') ORDER BY first_booking,second_booking;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A partitioned table routes rows into child tables according to a partition key. Range partition upper bounds are exclusive.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Very large time-based datasets may benefit from pruning and partition lifecycle operations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION BY declares a parent. CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF defines children and bounds. Unique constraints on a partitioned parent must include all partition key columns.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION BY declares a parent. CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF defines children and bounds. Unique constraints on a partitioned parent must include all partition key columns.

• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• INSERT names target columns and supplies matching values or a source query.
• CREATE TABLE declares names, types, defaults, and constraints as a durable contract.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Ordered aggregates retain a defined input order inside their aggregate call. A generated column derives its value from a row expression.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports need deterministic lists, and repeated row calculations can have a schema-level definition.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Write array_agg(value ORDER BY key). Stored generated columns persist calculated values; PostgreSQL 18 also supports virtual generated columns with additional restrictions. Use explicit STORED for this cross-version familiar example.

sections.title: Read the syntax

Write array_agg(value ORDER BY key). Stored generated columns persist calculated values; PostgreSQL 18 also supports virtual generated columns with additional restrictions. Use explicit STORED for this cross-version familiar example.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT category,array_agg(name ORDER BY id) AS product_names FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A gaps-and-islands query identifies runs of adjacent values. The grouping key can be built from the difference between a date and its ordered row number.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Usage streaks, consecutive reservations, and missing periods appear in many analytics tasks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: First remove duplicate dates at the intended grain. Number the ordered dates, subtract the row number in days, then group equal differences into islands.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
First remove duplicate dates at the intended grain. Number the ordered dates, subtract the row number in days, then group equal differences into islands.

• WITH gives a query stage a name; the final SELECT reads its output.
• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• OVER defines the partition, order, and optional frame for a window calculation.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT check_in AS day FROM bookings), numbered AS (SELECT day,day-(row_number() OVER(ORDER BY day))::integer AS grp FROM days) SELECT min(day) AS island_start,max(day) AS island_end,count(*) AS day_count FROM numbered GROUP BY grp ORDER BY island_start;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Using distinct booking check_in dates, return island_start, island_end, and day_count for runs of consecutive calendar days, ordered by island_start.
sections.code: WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT check_in AS day FROM bookings), numbered AS (SELECT day,day-(row_number() OVER(ORDER BY day))::integer AS grp FROM days) SELECT min(day) AS island_start,max(day) AS island_end,count(*) AS day_count FROM numbered GROUP BY grp ORDER BY island_start;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return day for dates from 2024-07-01 through 2024-07-07 with no orders, ordered by day.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An every-match query asks whether all required values have matching facts. This is sometimes called relational division.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A business may need customers who purchased every required category, or products satisfying every selected attribute.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Express every requirement as no missing requirement using nested NOT EXISTS, or compare the distinct matched count with a required count.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Express every requirement as no missing requirement using nested NOT EXISTS, or compare the distinct matched count with a required count.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT c.id,c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM (VALUES('Office'),('Tech')) required(category) WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id JOIN products p ON p.id=i.product_id WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' AND p.category=required.category)) ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id and name for customers with paid purchases in both Office and Tech categories, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT c.id,c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM (VALUES('Office'),('Tech')) required(category) WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id=o.id JOIN products p ON p.id=i.product_id WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' AND p.category=required.category)) ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return id and name of products containing both usb and work tags, ordered by id.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A percentile describes a position in an ordered distribution. percentile_cont interpolates; percentile_disc returns an actual input value.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Median and percentile metrics can describe skewed values more usefully than an average alone.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY expression) for ordered-set aggregates. A fraction such as 0.5 chooses the median. Cast approximate floating-point output to numeric before decimal rounding.

sections.title: Read the syntax

• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A professional customer report defines eligible orders, result grain, missing-value policy, and ordering before SQL is written.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Teams need one agreed meaning for revenue, repeat purchase, and customer value.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use paid orders only for revenue, preserve customers with no paid orders, and aggregate at the customer grain before ranking.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Use paid orders only for revenue, preserve customers with no paid orders, and aggregate at the customer grain before ranking.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• JOIN combines matching rows. ON defines the relationship; the join type decides which unmatched rows survive.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,c.name,count(o.id) AS paid_orders,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY revenue DESC,c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return customer_id, name, paid_orders, and revenue for every customer; revenue zero if none. Order revenue descending then customer_id.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,c.name,count(o.id) AS paid_orders,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY revenue DESC,c.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return category, revenue, and revenue_share as paid line revenue divided by all paid line revenue rounded to four decimals; order revenue descending then category.
sections.code: WITH sales AS (SELECT p.category,sum(i.quantity*i.unit_price) AS revenue FROM products p JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id=p.id JOIN orders o ON o.id=i.order_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category) SELECT category,revenue,round(revenue/NULLIF(sum(revenue) OVER(),0),4) AS revenue_share FROM sales ORDER BY revenue DESC,category;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A replenishment report compares available units with a business target and recent demand.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Stock decisions should distinguish unavailable items from slow or fast sellers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Compute demand at the product grain, then join it to every product. Keep zero-demand products visible.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Compute demand at the product grain, then join it to every product. Keep zero-demand products visible.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Hotel data uses intervals rather than isolated dates: a stay occupies nights from check-in through the day before checkout.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Occupancy and revenue depend on correct boundaries and per-night calculations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Expand stays into nights or use overlap predicates. An adjacent checkout and check-in can share the calendar date without sharing a night.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Expand stays into nights or use overlap predicates. An adjacent checkout and check-in can share the calendar date without sharing a night.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights,(check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate AS charge FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return id, guest, nights, and charge for each booking, ordered by id.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights,(check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate AS charge FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return day, occupied_rooms (distinct rooms), and revenue for July 1 through July 10 2024, including empty days; each occupied room contributes its booking nightly_rate. Order by day.
sections.code: SELECT d.day::date AS day,count(DISTINCT b.room) AS occupied_rooms,COALESCE(sum(b.nightly_rate),0) AS revenue FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-07-01',DATE '2024-07-10',INTERVAL '1 day') d(day) LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.check_in<=d.day::date AND b.check_out>d.day::date GROUP BY d.day ORDER BY d.day;

exercises.title: Occupancy against the known room roster
exercises.prompt: For July 1–7, 2024 return day, occupied_rooms, known_rooms, and occupancy_share rounded to four decimals. The known roster is every distinct room anywhere in bookings; occupied rooms cover the night using check_in<=day<check_out. Order by day.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT d.day::date AS day,count(DISTINCT b.room) AS occupied_rooms,r.n AS known_rooms,round(count(DISTINCT b.room)::numeric/NULLIF(r.n,0),4) AS occupancy_share FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-07-01',DATE '2024-07-07',INTERVAL '1 day') d(day) CROSS JOIN (SELECT count(DISTINCT room) AS n FROM bookings) r LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.check_in<=d.day::date AND b.check_out>d.day::date GROUP BY d.day,r.n ORDER BY d.day;
hints: Use checkout as an exclusive endpoint.
A room count is not the same as a booking count.
Clip durations before multiplying by a nightly rate.
exercises.explanation: Count distinct rooms rather than bookings to avoid double-counting a room. The stated roster assumption is essential; a production hotel needs an independent room inventory.

exercises.title: Recognize revenue only within a window
exercises.prompt: For each room, return room, recognized_nights, and recognized_revenue inside [2024-07-02,2024-07-05). Clip each booking to this interval; include rooms with zero recognized nights. Order by room.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT room,sum(greatest(least(check_out,DATE '2024-07-05')-greatest(check_in,DATE '2024-07-02'),0)) AS recognized_nights,sum(greatest(least(check_out,DATE '2024-07-05')-greatest(check_in,DATE '2024-07-02'),0)*nightly_rate) AS recognized_revenue FROM bookings GROUP BY room ORDER BY room;
hints: Use checkout as an exclusive endpoint.
A room count is not the same as a booking count.
Clip durations before multiplying by a nightly rate.
exercises.explanation: Intersect stay boundaries with the reporting window, clamp a negative duration to zero, then apply the nightly rate before grouping rooms.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An analytics metric needs a numerator, denominator, time range, and unit of analysis.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A conversion rate can change merely because the analyst counts events rather than people.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Aggregate first at the chosen grain. Keep distinct people separate from event counts and make missing periods explicit.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Aggregate first at the chosen grain. Keep distinct people separate from event counts and make missing periods explicit.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT payload->>'device' AS device,count(*) AS event_count,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customer_count FROM events GROUP BY device ORDER BY device;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return device, event_count, and customer_count as distinct customers for all events, ordered by device.
sections.code: SELECT payload->>'device' AS device,count(*) AS event_count,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customer_count FROM events GROUP BY device ORDER BY device;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return cohort_month (first day of customer join month), customer_count (all joined customers), and paid_revenue including zero, ordered by cohort_month.
sections.code: WITH customer_revenue AS (SELECT c.id,c.joined_on,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS revenue FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id) SELECT date_trunc('month',joined_on)::date AS cohort_month,count(*) AS customer_count,sum(revenue) AS paid_revenue FROM customer_revenue GROUP BY cohort_month ORDER BY cohort_month;

exercises.title: First purchase after a first visit
exercises.prompt: For customers who have a visit event, return customer_id, first_visit, and first_purchase_after_visit. The purchase is the earliest purchase timestamp at or after their first visit, or NULL if none exists. Order by customer_id.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH visits AS (SELECT customer_id,min(occurred_at) AS first_visit FROM events WHERE kind='visit' GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT v.customer_id,v.first_visit,(SELECT min(e.occurred_at) FROM events e WHERE e.customer_id=v.customer_id AND e.kind='purchase' AND e.occurred_at>=v.first_visit) AS first_purchase_after_visit FROM visits v ORDER BY v.customer_id;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A reliable report combines correct calculations, deterministic results, documented assumptions, and checks for edge cases.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Professional SQL work is reviewed and maintained by people who did not write its first version.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Break the report into named stages, test empty and duplicate cases, compare totals, inspect a plan, and communicate which facts the data can support.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body:
Break the report into named stages, test empty and duplicate cases, compare totals, inspect a plan, and communicate which facts the data can support.

• SELECT lists output expressions in the requested column order. AS introduces a result alias.
• FROM names the input relation. Short aliases qualify columns when names could be ambiguous.
• WHERE keeps only rows where its Boolean condition is true, before grouping or windows.
• GROUP BY chooses the result grain; aggregate functions summarize each group.
• ORDER BY establishes output order. Later keys resolve ties in earlier keys.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,count(*) AS paid_orders,sum(total) AS paid_revenue,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Return month_start, paid_orders, paid_revenue, and unique_customers for paid orders, counting known distinct customers only; order by month_start.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,count(*) AS paid_orders,sum(total) AS paid_revenue,count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Return order_id, header_total, line_total, and difference (header minus line total) for all orders, with a zero line total if no lines; order by order_id.
sections.code: WITH lines AS (SELECT order_id,sum(quantity*unit_price) AS line_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT o.id AS order_id,o.total AS header_total,COALESCE(l.line_total,0) AS line_total,o.total-COALESCE(l.line_total,0) AS difference FROM orders o LEFT JOIN lines l ON l.order_id=o.id ORDER BY o.id;

exercises.title: Explain a revenue reconciliation mismatch
exercises.prompt: A paid-order report sums orders.total. A line report sums quantity*unit_price after joining order_items. Their totals differ. Explain at least four checks you would perform before changing either query. This answer is self-assessed; no English string matching is used.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT true AS discussed;
hints: Compare the exact eligible order sets and result grains.
Look for missing lines, duplicate joins, guest customers, and different status or date predicates.
Consider business amounts outside line prices, such as tax, delivery, discounts, and refunds.
exercises.explanation: Use the worked explanation as a review rubric, then mark the exercise reviewed only when your explanation covers both SQL correctness and business definitions.
exercises.modelAnswer: First compare status and time filters so both reports use the same eligible orders. Check whether inner joins remove guest or line-less orders. Verify join cardinality so header totals are not repeated for each line and lines are not duplicated by another relationship. Reconcile per order before comparing grand totals. Check whether header totals include tax, shipping, discounts, refunds, or rounding that line totals exclude. Inspect NULL handling and currency units. Preserve a deterministic per-order discrepancy report and confirm the intended business definition with the report owner.

exercises.title: Year-to-date paid revenue
exercises.prompt: Return month_start, revenue, and year_to_date from paid orders. Aggregate by month, then accumulate revenue within each calendar year in month order. Order by month_start.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH monthly AS (SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month_start) SELECT month_start,revenue,sum(revenue) OVER(PARTITION BY extract(year FROM month_start) ORDER BY month_start ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS year_to_date FROM monthly ORDER BY month_start;
hints: Fix the eligible paid-order set before combining facts.
Never sum a header measure at line-item grain.
Reconcile at order grain before rolling the result up to months.
exercises.explanation: Aggregate detail orders before running the window. Partitioning by year resets the accumulated total at a year boundary.

exercises.title: Monthly header-to-line reconciliation
exercises.prompt: For paid orders, return month_start, paid_orders, header_revenue, line_revenue, and difference (header minus lines). Include guest orders and orders with no lines. Aggregate line totals per order before joining; order by month_start.
exercises.solutionSQL: WITH lines AS (SELECT order_id,sum(quantity*unit_price) AS amount FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT date_trunc('month',o.ordered_on)::date AS month_start,count(*) AS paid_orders,sum(o.total) AS header_revenue,sum(COALESCE(l.amount,0)) AS line_revenue,sum(o.total)-sum(COALESCE(l.amount,0)) AS difference FROM orders o LEFT JOIN lines l ON l.order_id=o.id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;
hints: Fix the eligible paid-order set before combining facts.
Never sum a header measure at line-item grain.
Reconcile at order grain before rolling the result up to months.
exercises.explanation: Preaggregating lines prevents repeating a header total once per line. LEFT JOIN keeps line-less orders, and no customer join discards guest revenue.
